newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW - Ewart confident on Belfast dockland site.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ewart confident on Belfast dockland site.

text.p: Ewart Plc, the property company behind plans to turn a patch of Belfast dockland into Northern Ireland's premier business address, remains optimistic about the 130 million pound ($219.6 million) Lanyon Place development despite renewed guerilla violence.

Irish Republican Army guerrillas launched a rocket attack on Belfast's High Court on Monday, a few hundred yards (metres) from Lanyon Place, lightly injuring two people, in the latest attack since the collapse of the IRA's ceasefire last February.
"I said last February when the ceasefire broke that it simply made our job very much more difficult and that continues to be the case," Ewart chief executive Barry Gilligan told Reuters.
"But that doesn't mean we have given up or we are not trying. Yes, I would concede it's more difficult but not impossible," he said.
Lanyon Place, a 16-acre riverside site formerly known as Laganbank, houses Belfast's latest landmark -- Waterfront Hall, a domed circular concert hall which opens on January 17.

A four-star 187-bedroom Hilton Hotel is under construction at the site which will also include British Telecom's regional headquarters as well as bars, restaurants and 300,000 square feet of office space.
Gilligan says that of the end-development value of 130 million pounds, 80 million is already committed and another 10 million is in the pipeline.

Ewart is in the detailed planning stage for the retail site and hopes to proceed with it this year. The company is also in talks with three parties interested in renting office space but nothing firm has yet been signed.
Meanwhile, Gilligan noted that Hilton began negotiations about the Belfast project before the IRA's 1994 ceasefire and remains totally committed to the development.

"Hilton's interest has never waned. Even with the unravelling of the ceasefire over the last 12 months Hilton have never questioned or regretted their decision to go ahead," says Gilligan, who remains convinced that the site will be fully developed ahead of schedule.
"We had dark days before, there may be more dark days before we're finished but on balance I think the potential for this site is enormous."
Ewart, which began as a producer and exporter of fine Irish linen in 1814, also remains committed to doing more business in Northern Ireland.

"We continue, as we have done over the years, to look at other opportunities in Northern Ireland. There are a few we're looking at which I'm not in a position to elaborate further on at this time," he said.
"We do also look in England and Scotland but we have not in any sense shied away from Northern Ireland because of the events of recent months."
The company is particularly interested in further expanding its car park business. It acquired Strand Parking Limited last August and now manages 40 sites throughout Britain.

"We are expanding both by involving ourselves in more management contracts and by the acquisition of multi-storey car parks. We are very much in the market for those at the moment throughout these islands," Gilligan said ,adding he hoped to make an announcement in this regard in the very near future.
Ewart is also interested in developing its hotel business, provided the hotel operator is an equity partner in the project.

"We have a number of sites in Belfast which lend themselves to the development of hotels," Gilligan said, adding that the company is currently talking to a number of people in Britain and Ireland about its Great Victoria Street and Bedford Street sites in Belfast.
